title: Needle-felted chaffinch
subtitle: A male chaffinch in rust, slate-blue, and white merino
excerpt: Needle felt a male chaffinch with its rust-orange breast, slate-blue cap, greenish back, and white double wing bars. The finished bird is about 6 cm beak to tail and is recognisable at a glance from across a room.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional British needle-felting guild practice. Garden bird forms are standard beginner subjects; the chaffinch's distinct markings make it a popular project.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dry felting method using barbed needles to lock wool fibres together without heat or water.
Wool drawn into a continuous ribbon; the standard input material for needle-felting.

content.text: has two marks that make it instantly recognisable: the double white wing bars and the warm rust-orange breast. The blue-grey cap completes the face once the body colour is set. The body is the same compact oval as a robin but slightly longer. Work each colour section cleanly in sequence using fine
layers, and needle the wing bars last so they sit on the surface of the wing rather than sinking in.

attrs.title: Needle safety
attrs.body: Stab straight in and out at 90 degrees. Keep the finger guard on the supporting hand throughout.

items.name: Slate-blue or blue-grey merino roving (cap, nape)
Strong thread and needle for bead eyes

content.text: Roll the green roving into a core body about 5.5 cm long, compact and firm. The chaffinch body is a blunt oval, fuller at the breast end and tapering to a narrower tail. Needle felt on all sides until the core holds its shape without a hand supporting it.

Apply rust-orange roving across the front and sides of the body, from the chin to the belly. The rust colour extends around the flanks in chaffinches; needle it a little further round than you might expect. Keep the breast surface even and the upper edge clean where it will meet the blue cap.

Roll a head ball from green roving and attach it to the body at the neck. Apply slate-blue roving over the top of the head and down to the back of the neck. The cap is not purely blue: the forehead has a slight greenish or yellowish tinge in real chaffinches, which you can reproduce by needling a thin layer of olive roving over the brow before the blue layer goes on. Shape a short conical bill from a pinch of dark grey roving.

Needle two flat wing shapes from brown-chestnut roving against the sides of the body. Work the wings into the shoulder area by needling through the wing base into the body. Once the wings are attached, needle two thin parallel lines of white roving across each wing to form the double wing bars. The wing bars are the most recognisable field mark; keep them parallel and at slightly different angles from each other as they are in the live bird.

Stitch the bead eyes into position on the head, just behind the bill and slightly to the sides. Needle a dark grey or black tail at the rear of the body. Trim any loose surface fibres and check the wing bars are still visible and not obscured by surface fuzz.

items.problem: The wing bars sank into the wing surface
items.cause: The white roving was needled too deeply, pushing it below the wing surface layer
items.fix: Apply white roving in a thin strip and needle only on the surface, using the fine needle at a very shallow angle. Let the wing surface carry the white on top rather than inside.

items.problem: The cap colour bleeds into the breast colour
items.cause: The two colour sections were applied too close together before either was firmly needled
items.fix: Fully needle each colour section before adding the adjacent one. A firmly compacted surface accepts a top-layer colour without the colours mixing.
